stories.summary: In Game 14 of the World Championship, Ding was a pawn down in a rook-and-bishop endgame that is a theoretical draw unless both rooks and both bishops come off. At move 52 a bishop trade was impossible: the white bishop could step away, and Gukesh's king was two squares too far to support his bishop. By move 54 both conditions had quietly changed. The white bishop was on a8 with only one diagonal open, and Gukesh's king had moved up. Ding, already thinking ahead to the rapid tiebreak where he was the favourite, played 55. Rf2, allowing a rook trade followed by a forced bishop trade. Gukesh did not see it either at first. He said he was about to play Rb3. Then he spotted it, and only after watching Gukesh's reaction did Ding realise what he had done.
stories.insight: The blunder was not a calculation failure. It was a failure to notice that the world had changed. Two elite grandmasters were both stuck in the old equilibrium, just as people get stuck with fixed views of their careers or their partners.
stories.quote: So both these super strong grandmasters were stuck in the old equilibrium. Neither of them realize what has happened.

stories.topic: Gukesh's Plan: Make Every Game Long
stories.summary: Ding came in poorly prepared in two ways. He had a small team, so he was often surprised in the opening and burned an hour or more recovering. He was also not physically fit. Amit recalls a factoid from his junior days: in a five-hour classical game, a player burns as many calories as a boxer does in a round. Anand did yoga, and Carlsen and Gukesh play sports. Gukesh noticed Ding looked tired and deliberately dragged every game out. In Game 6, Ding was slightly better and offered a draw by threefold repetition, and Gukesh, in the worse position, declined it to keep playing. Fatigue finally showed at the end of Game 14.
stories.insight: At the top, raw skill is roughly equal. What decides outcomes is preparation, fitness and attitude, the game outside the game.
stories.quote: Gukesh said he was looking tired, so we decided I will make him play for as long as possible.

stories.topic: Gukesh's Global Team and the Teenager Who Joined Anyway
stories.summary: On Anand's suggestion, Gukesh made Grzegorz Gajewski, Anand's former second, his head of team. Jan-Krzysztof Duda played more than 300 practice games with him. Radosław Wojtaszek and Harikrishna also joined, which Amit calls 'a slight Polish band.' The seconds worked from Spain on a time-zone schedule so they could prepare while Gukesh slept. Gukesh did not invite Indian peers like Arjun, Pragg or Nihal, who are natural rivals. Yet a 16- or 17-year-old German talent, Vincent Keymer, trained by Peter Leko and himself a potential future rival, joined for the learning. Amit credits two of the match's most spectacular opening ideas to Keymer.
stories.insight: A great attitude can override narrow rivalry logic. Keymer chose learning over guarding territory, and the team as a whole was built for the job rather than for comfort.
stories.quote: Vincent Keymer, however, had a different attitude. He had a great attitude. He's like, I will learn a lot from this and let me go in for the experience.

stories.summary: Gukesh's early coach Vishnu Prasanna proposed an experiment to his parents: train the boy without chess engines. Until Gukesh became a grandmaster, he reportedly used no computers at all. Today his calculation in complex middlegames is unmatched; Carlsen has said Gukesh finds lines in post-mortems that never crossed his mind. The flip side, critics such as Carlsen say, is odd positional intuition. Amit suspects this may also be because Gukesh skipped the online blitz grind of 2020-21, when other Indians filled the top spots at Titled Tuesday. His rapid and blitz ratings sit 100-150 points below the elite.
stories.insight: How you are trained leaves fingerprints. Forcing yourself to work things out without a crutch can build unusual depth, at the price of gaps elsewhere.
stories.quote: Let's do an experiment. Let's train him without computers.

stories.summary: Players who cross 2700 usually get invited to elite round-robins. There you press with White, settle for draws with Black, and 6/10 is a decent score. Arjun got few invites because India already had Pragg, Vidit, Nihal and Harikrishna in that circuit, and organisers won't invite four Indians to a ten-player event planned a year ahead. So he played Swiss-system opens against 2600-2650 grandmasters. Every draw there cost him rating points, so he had to try to win every game. He developed a wild, risk-taking style that Carlsen called that of a madman, and rose from about 2700 to a live peak of 2809, world number two. Amit compares the dominance to Bobby Fischer's 6-0 wins over Taimanov and Larsen.
stories.insight: Arjun didn't choose his style. A structural constraint forced it on him, and it made him unique.
stories.quote: in an open tournament you have to try to win every freaking game.

stories.topic: Srinath's Board-Three Gambit at the Olympiad
stories.summary: At the 2024 Olympiad, Arjun was India's top-rated player, but team coach Srinath Narayanan put him on board three rather than board one. His logic was that Arjun is brilliant at beating 2600s and board three is where he would face them. If everyone else just drew, India would still win. Arjun dominated, and Gukesh scored around 10/11 on top board. That included a miraculous endgame win against Wei Yi, then the top Chinese player with the world's best performance rating, which even Hikaru Nakamura praised. Both the open and women's teams won gold.
stories.insight: Smart strategy puts people where their specific edge pays off most, not where hierarchy says they belong.
stories.quote: Why board three? Because he's brilliant at beating twenty six hundreds, and board three is where he's likely to play them.

stories.topic: 'But Don't Come for Class Anymore' (The Disciple)
stories.summary: In Chaitanya Tamhane's film, Sharad Nerulkar is a purist Hindustani classical singer and teacher. A student's mother says her son wants to join a college fusion band, with one singer doing Western rock and her son doing classical. The boy won't join without his guru's permission, and the mother clearly wants him to. Nerulkar tells the boy he can join. After a silence, he adds that the boy should stop coming to class.
stories.insight: The choice is not about an activity. It is about identity. Doing something repeatedly changes the kind of person you become.
stories.quote: So Nerulkar turns to the boy and he says, Yes, you can join them. Moment of silence, and then he adds, But don't come for class anymore.

stories.topic: Why Magnus Walked Away From the Crown
stories.summary: Carlsen did not quit the classical World Championship out of petulance. Before each title match, against Caruana, Karjakin and Nepomniachtchi, he and his team spent six months in prep camps memorising engine lines. If an opponent steered into a line he hadn't memorised, he could lose. He concluded his quality of life had gone to bits and that it wasn't really chess anymore. He moved to rapid and blitz, and now to 'freestyle' (Fischer Random, or Chess960), which Bobby Fischer devised in the 1970s out of the same frustration. Carlsen has already lost two Chess960 world titles, to Wesley So and Hikaru Nakamura, but plays anyway.
stories.insight: Carlsen gave up guaranteed dominance in exchange for the joy of the game, choosing renewal over mastery.
stories.quote: This is not even chess. This is mugging up, mugging up, mugging up. The joy of playing chess isn't there.

stories.summary: At the 2022 Sinquefield Cup, Carlsen lost to American GM Hans Niemann, withdrew, and called him a cheat. Niemann had admitted to cheating online on Chess.com as a 14- or 15-year-old but said that was in the past. Amit first gave Carlsen the benefit of the doubt, but stopped within a few months. Nobody ever offered a plausible mechanism for cheating over the board: broadcasts run on a delay, and players are checked for devices. The 'vibrating anal beads' theory, which Elon Musk retweeted, was never serious. Carlsen never apologised. At the recent World Blitz quarterfinal, Niemann won game two against him, and Carlsen's hands visibly shook in game three before he won games three and four.
stories.insight: Because the accuser was Magnus, the burden of proof quietly shifted onto the accused, which is exactly backwards.
stories.quote: Because extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. If somebody is cheating over the board, you gotta tell me how.

stories.summary: At the World Rapid in New York, Carlsen scored only 2.5/5 on day one and turned up on day two in jeans, which breaks the dress code every player signs. Ian Nepomniachtchi had already been asked to change out of sneakers and did. Carlsen's hotel was three minutes away, and he was given until round nine to change. He refused 'on principle,' so FIDE would not pair him. He withdrew from both the Rapid and the Blitz and swore at FIDE on Take Take Take. He then went over the heads of CEO Emil Sutovsky and vice-president Vishy Anand to FIDE president Arkady Dvorkovich and was let back into the Blitz in jeans. He said there were 'no grown-ups in FIDE' and that Anand was not up to his job.
stories.insight: Amit doubts the tantrum would have happened if Carlsen had been winning. A bad mood plus star power turned a dress code into an ego war.
stories.quote: what is this principle that on principle you refuse to follow a rule.

stories.topic: The Shared Blitz Title and the 'Short Draws' Clip
stories.summary: In the World Blitz final, Carlsen won the first two games against Nepomniachtchi, and Nepo came back with a brilliancy to level it. Three sudden-death games were drawn. Carlsen then proposed splitting the title, Nepo agreed, and the arbiter went to consult FIDE. Dvorkovich allowed it. A ChessBase India video of the waiting period later caught Carlsen telling Nepo that if FIDE refused, they should just play one short draw after another. Sutovsky called out the behaviour, and Carlsen said he had been joking.
stories.insight: Hundreds of players travelled to New York for a tournament that should have a winner. Once a system has bent for one powerful person, everyone becomes afraid to say no.
stories.quote: It's basically a kind of match fixing.

stories.topic: Havel on Free Speech (via Salil Tripathi)
stories.summary: At a press conference, journalist Salil Tripathi asked Václav Havel, then Czechoslovakia's head of state, about the argument that feeding people matters more than free speech. Havel said free speech is the most important right, then asked who argues otherwise. Salil replied that it was Lee Kuan Yew, whom Havel was meeting that afternoon. After a silence, Havel said he would make sure to tell him he was wrong.
stories.insight: A principled person holds the same line when it is diplomatically awkward.
stories.quote: Because without free speech, how will a hungry man even be able to communicate that he's hungry?

stories.summary: During President Nelson Mandela's tour of Asian countries, while Aung San Suu Kyi was still imprisoned, Salil Tripathi asked whether he would protest her treatment. Mandela conferred with aides and said no. Salil pressed him: when Mandela was in prison, people like Salil had spoken up for him, so why not speak for her? Mandela's reply was that this was a different Mandela now.
stories.insight: Amit calls the answer glib and disgusting. It is a vivid example of how power changes people who once claimed principles.
stories.quote: that was prisoner Mandela. This is President Mandela. I'm imprisoned by the presidency.

stories.topic: The Blunder Seen Through the Engine
stories.summary: Amit watched 55. Rf2 on Sagar Shah's stream. The moment it was played, the engine evaluation swung and everyone stood up. Only Tania Sachdev, he says, worked it out from the board, and even Sagar glanced at the computer to confirm. On David Howell's broadcast, which had no engine evaluation, Howell took about as long as Gukesh to see the blunder because he was thinking for himself. Amit also bristles at audiences who clap whenever a player finds the engine's top move.
stories.insight: Technology meant to illuminate can stop you from actually experiencing and understanding the game.
stories.quote: Howell took as much time to figure out it's a blunder as Gukesh did. You can actually time them.

stories.topic: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal, the Long Game
stories.summary: Sagar Shah, an International Master who never made GM, and his wife Amruta Mokal ran ChessBase India for years as a labour of love. Sagar filmed on his mobile phone, went to under-11 and district events, interviewed small kids and women players without hesitation, and saw little growth for three to five years. During Covid, with comedian Samay Raina's help, the channel exploded and now has millions of subscribers. A clip shows an 11-year-old Gukesh telling Sagar he wants to be the youngest world champion. Another shows Sagar explaining positions to kids sitting on the floor, Gukesh among them. The morning after the 2024 title, Sagar and Amruta flew to Singapore, and Gukesh hugged both of them.
stories.insight: Amit would give them the second 'Bharat Ratna for chess' after Anand. Building something for love, without overthinking the market, can shape a whole ecosystem.
stories.quote: Often he would just go and he would shoot with his mobile phone, using the sound of the mobile phone.

core_ideas.explanation: Ding's blunder came from a frozen mental model, not from bad calculation. The same thing happens in life. Your specialty gets automated while you aren't watching, or a couple stops noticing how each other has changed and becomes 'strangers in the same house.' You can't update your priors every minute, but you should watch for the moment the king has moved two squares.
core_ideas.quote: mentally all the time we get stuck with one view of the world, and then everything changes, and we don't realize that it has changed.

core_ideas.concept: Overestimate the Short Term, Underestimate the Long Term
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's framing of status quo bias. We wave away novel developments as overblown, which makes big shifts feel sudden when they finally land. Waking up and changing course is one of life's great skills.
core_ideas.quote: The great philosopher Bill Gates says that the world changes by less than you think in one year and more than you think in 10 years.

core_ideas.explanation: The worst hiking accidents happen near the end. Tom Vanderbilt finds the same for traffic accidents close to home. Ding's mind had already moved on to the tiebreak. The sharpness you bring at move 10 fades by move 50, and that is exactly when you're most vulnerable.
core_ideas.quote: the worst accidents happened when you think you've almost reached home. You know, you let your guard down.

core_ideas.explanation: Excellence alone entitles you to nothing. Preparation, team, physical fitness and a fighting attitude decided the World Championship more than the moves did.
core_ideas.quote: being good is not enough. It's the stuff that goes around it that matters. It's the game outside the game.

core_ideas.concept: Hire for the Job, Not the Tribe
core_ideas.explanation: An all-Indian team with the comfort of familiar relationships would have been easy. Gukesh's team was almost entirely foreign, chosen to fix specific weaknesses; Duda, for instance, is a top rapid player. Ajay's lesson for Indian firms: assemble global talent around the task.
core_ideas.quote: They didn't think in terms of nationality. They just said we've got to get a job done.

core_ideas.explanation: Anand made Gukesh possible. He passed on knowledge and culture, and even suggested Gajewski as head of the team. Each generation is helped, and also limited, by the one before it, and then hands down something better.
core_ideas.quote: the limitations of the people who came before are an upper bound on what we can do.

core_ideas.concept: What You Do Shapes Who You Are
core_ideas.explanation: Gukesh's computer-free training and Arjun's forced diet of opens shaped them into very different players. The same holds for the rest of us. Our company, our habits, and whether we spend time scrolling or reading and watching good cinema all shape our character. Each choice is really about who we want to be.
core_ideas.quote: It's not about what you want to do. It's who do you want to be.

core_ideas.concept: Know the Oddities of Your Origin Story
core_ideas.explanation: Everyone's path leaves them with particular strengths and blind spots. Without whining or beating yourself up, map them. Then decide whether to compensate for weaknesses (longer lives make us more malleable) or to make big bets on your strengths.
core_ideas.quote: it is interesting and important for us to be self aware of the oddities of our own origin story.

core_ideas.concept: How Engines Turned Classical Chess Into Memorisation
core_ideas.explanation: Engine evaluations assume perfect play from both sides, and humans never play perfectly. So elite preparation has become a hunt for deliberately suboptimal deviations that only a computer could refute, which pushes opponents out of their memorised lines. Theory has grown exponentially, and every newcomer faces a mountain of it before getting to actually play.
core_ideas.quote: deviate somewhere with a move that is not the optimal move, but to which the riposte can only be found by another computer, and not by a human on the board.

core_ideas.concept: Mastery Is Good, Renewal Is Better
core_ideas.explanation: People master one form and then run on autopilot, like a brain surgeon who stops reading new papers. Carlsen chose the joy of fresh play over guaranteed dominance. Ajay adds that longer lifespans make spending a lifetime in one unchanging trade far drearier.
core_ideas.quote: Mastery is good, renewal is better.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay worries that Chess960 strips away the familiar board that lets casual fans follow along. Amit replies that casual fans never really read classical positions either. Strong commentators like David Howell, Peter Svidler and Tania Sachdev are the bridge in either format.
core_ideas.quote: my proposition to you is that without great commentary, we would be as lost

core_ideas.explanation: Carlsen's dominance, status and business clout preceded his worst behaviour. Amit warns he risks becoming Kramnik, a great champion now an embittered accuser of Nakamura, Naroditsky and Gukesh. Much of success is luck. The model for handling power is Anand: powerful, but soft-spoken and working behind the scenes.
core_ideas.quote: Do you think Vishy Anand doesn't have power? Oh man, he has power. But you would never know.

core_ideas.concept: Judge the Act, Not the Name
core_ideas.explanation: Borrowing a line from Hans Niemann: strip away the speaker's identity and evaluate what was said or done. Forget that it's the world number one and ask whether the behaviour is acceptable from anyone.
core_ideas.quote: forget it is Magnus Carlsen, forget it's the greatest player of all time, forget it is the world number one. Is it appropriate behavior?

core_ideas.explanation: Engine bars teach viewers to react to numbers instead of understanding positions. AI can be used the same way. Use ChatGPT for ideas and polish, but do the writing yourself so your brain keeps working.
core_ideas.quote: If you use it as a crutch, you dumb yourself down.

core_ideas.concept: Love and a Bias for Action
core_ideas.explanation: Sagar and Amruta never asked whether there was a market or whether they were good enough. They kept showing up for years out of love for chess. People overthink new ventures. Amit's prescription is to act.
core_ideas.quote: act today, have a bias for action, do what you love, things will work out.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's addendum: movements need more than the direct doers like Anand and WestBridge. They also need people who tend the community and keep morale and enthusiasm alive. It takes a village.
core_ideas.quote: there is a tremendous role for the community organizer people.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: A wink at their own course name: Amit on calling everything 'life lessons': 'Well I mean, why not? We haven't trademarked it because like who cares?'
Ajay introducing a familiar maxim with a straight face: 'The great philosopher Bill Gates says...'
Amit's Hindi riff on overestimating the short term, the 'sab badal jayega... viral ho jayega' (everything will change, it'll go viral) fantasy, followed by: 'nothing happens.'
On Gukesh's seconds Gajewski, Duda and Wojtaszek: 'Slight Polish band kind of happening here.'
Ajay on the cosier alternative of an all-Indian team: 'the comfort of the relationships and sharing biryani at night.'
Amit on outwitting your opponent at chess, 'the way I outwit you the one time we played chess, Ajay, and is there on record as well.'
Amit on audiences clapping when Gukesh found the engine's top move: 'Are you guys morons? There are probably four or five moves which are fine here.'
Carlsen, per Amit, went on Take Take Take and said 'Fuck you' to FIDE 'in exactly these many words', and later complained there are 'no grown-ups in FIDE.'
Jeansgate: Carlsen's refusal to change out of jeans at the New York World Rapid. Amit notes Jimmy Carter famously made jeans acceptable as president, adding RIP since he had passed recently.
The 'vibrating anal beads' theory of how Niemann might have cheated, retweeted by Elon Musk. Amit: 'shit like that was never serious.'
The Russian chess federation's allegation that Ding threw the World Championship, which Amit rejects.
Chess as a physical sport: from Amit's junior days, the factoid that a five-hour classical game burns as many calories as a boxer uses in a round. Anand famously did yoga to stay fit.
Peter Leko, Keymer's coach, once led Kramnik 6-5 in a World Championship match. Kramnik won the last game to tie, and as the incumbent kept the title, 'bit of a tragedy.'
Alexander Grischuk, notorious for severe time trouble in classical chess yet twice world blitz champion, as proof that classical time pressure differs from blitz.
Bobby Fischer's 6-0 sweeps of Taimanov and Larsen, and his win over Petrosian, as the closest parallel to Arjun's dominance of 2600-level grandmasters.

Chess960 (Fischer Random): Bobby Fischer's 1970s answer to opening drudgery, with back-rank pieces shuffled identically for both sides across 960 possible starts. Carlsen rebrands it as 'freestyle.' Amit on classical chess: reports of its death are exaggerated.
'Power corrupts, absolute power corrupts absolutely', which Amit widens from governments to anyone with power and success.
Amit's hypothetical Bharat Ratna for chess: the first to Vishy Anand, the second jointly to Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal.
